passages.happening:
“On the first day of the second month of the second year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt, the LORD spoke to Moses in the Tent of Meeting in the Wilderness of Sinai” (verse 1).

God tells Moses and Aaron to count the people: ‘listing every man by name, one by one’ (verse 2). They are to count the men ‘twenty years of age or older’ who can serve in the army (verse 3). One leader from each tribe is to help, and the twelve are named (verses 5-15).

Moses and Aaron gather the whole congregation that same day and record each man by his clan and family, ‘just as the LORD had commanded Moses’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The book opens exactly one month after the tabernacle was set up (Exodus 40:17). Israel is still camped at the foot of Mount Sinai. The covenant has been made, the law given, and God's tent stands in the middle of the camp.

Until now Israel has been a crowd of freed slaves. A census turns a crowd into an ordered people. Ancient states counted their people for taxes, for labor and for war, and texts from the city of Mari in Syria, from the eighteenth century BC, describe tribal groups being called up for military service. This count is for the army. Only men of twenty and over are listed, and the phrase that keeps returning is those ‘who could serve in the army’. The land ahead would not simply be walked into.

Notice how the counting is done. It follows the layers of Israel's life: the father's household, then the clan, then the tribe. And each man is named. The Hebrew verb for counting here, paqad, means more than adding up. It can mean to muster, to appoint, to take note of. God is taking stock of his people and giving each a place.

The names of the twelve leaders are old in style. Many are built on the names El and Shaddai, such as Elizur and Zurishaddai, and none contains a form of the name Yahweh, the LORD, which became common in Israelite names later. Some scholars take this as a sign of old tradition. Others think a later writer could have used old-style names.

One of the twelve is worth marking. Nahshon son of Amminadab leads the tribe of Judah (verse 7).
passages.later:
God had promised Abraham offspring like the stars: “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able” (Genesis 15:5). Now Abraham's family is large enough to be counted tribe by tribe.

Nahshon appears again in the family line of King David (Ruth 4:20) and in Matthew's list of the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:4).

God speaks of knowing his people by name. Through Isaiah he says, ‘I have called you by your name; you are Mine’ (Isaiah 43:1). Jesus says of the good shepherd, “He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3).
passages.asks: God had every man listed by name, one by one. Ask whether you think of yourself as known to God by name, or as one more face in a crowd. And ask whose name you could learn this week, among people you usually pass without noticing.

passages.happening:
The tribes are counted one at a time, each in the same words. Reuben comes first, as ‘the firstborn of Israel’: “those registered to the tribe of Reuben numbered 46,500” (verse 21). Eleven more totals follow. Judah is the largest, with 74,600 (verse 27). Manasseh is the smallest, with 32,200 (verse 35).

“And all those counted totaled 603,550” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
The chapter repeats itself on purpose. Each tribe is given the same formula: its name, its clans and families, the age, the army, the total. Lists in the ancient world were often written this way. The effect is that no tribe is passed over. Each is counted with the same care, from the largest to the smallest.

The twelve tribes come from the twelve sons of Jacob. But Levi is not counted here, and the number is still twelve. That is because Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, are counted as separate tribes. Jacob had adopted them as his own (Genesis 48:5).

A first hearer would also have heard the list with the end of the book in mind. This is the generation that came out of Egypt. In chapter 26 Moses will count again, nearly forty years later, and not one of these men will be on the second list except Caleb and Joshua. The whole book turns on the difference between the two counts.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the same total when it counts the silver each man paid for the tabernacle: ‘a total of 603,550 men’ (Exodus 38:26).

Moses later reminded Israel that their numbers were never the reason God chose them: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7).

The last book of the Bible echoes this chapter. John hears the number of God's servants who are sealed, counted tribe by tribe (Revelation 7:4-8).
passages.hard:
Could there really have been 603,550 men of fighting age in the wilderness? With women and children that would mean two million people or more.

Christians read this in more than one way. Some take the number as it stands. They note that the tribal totals add up exactly, that it agrees with the figure in Exodus (Exodus 12:37; 38:26), that Israel had multiplied greatly in Egypt (Exodus 1:7), and that God's power is not limited by what seems likely.

Others point out that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit. Verse 16 of this chapter uses it that way, for ‘the clans of Israel’, and Gideon uses the same word when he says, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). Read that way, the fighting force would be far smaller. Several scholars have worked out versions of this reading, among them George Mendenhall (1958) and Colin Humphreys (1998). Still others take the figures as symbolic, or as a later count set back into the wilderness years.

Each reading has its difficulty. The first must explain how so great a number fits what is known of the land, and how it fits Moses' own words that Israel was ‘the fewest of all peoples’ (Deuteronomy 7:7). The second must explain why the lists add up as if they were thousands.

Christians who hold Scripture as God's word are found on more than one side, and these notes take no side. The note on Exodus 12:37 sets out the same question. On every reading the chapter's claim is the same: God has made Abraham's family into a people and is making them ready for the land he promised.
passages.asks: Every tribe was counted with the same care, the smallest with the largest. Ask where you are tempted to measure a church, a family or yourself by size. And ask what it would mean to believe Moses' words, that God's choice of his people never rested on their numbers.

passages.happening:
The tribe of Levi is left out of the count. God had told Moses, “Do not number the tribe of Levi in the census with the other Israelites” (verse 49).

The Levites have a different task. “They shall carry the tabernacle and all its articles, care for it, and camp around it” (verse 50). They take it down when the camp moves and set it up when the camp stops. “Any outsider who goes near it must be put to death” (verse 51).

The other tribes camp further out, each under its own banner. The Levites camp around the tabernacle, ‘so that no wrath will fall on the congregation of Israel’ (verse 53).

“Thus the Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 54).
passages.hearers:
The Levites were not counted for war because their service was the tent itself. They took it apart, carried it, put it up again and guarded it.

The warning in verse 51 sounds harsh to a modern ear. The ‘outsider’ is anyone who is not a Levite, an ordinary Israelite who wanders in among the holy things. Leviticus had already shown how serious this was. On the first day of the priests' service, two of Aaron's sons died for coming near to God in a way he had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1-2). God's presence in the camp was Israel's greatest gift, and it was not safe to treat it carelessly.

So the Levites' camp is a protection. They stand between the tent and the tribes, like a guard set for the people's sake. The aim is stated: that no wrath should fall on Israel. The arrangement exists so that God can live in the middle of his people without harm coming to them.

The chapter ends on a note that will soon sound sad. Israel ‘did everything just as the LORD had commanded’. This first generation begins the book with obedience. A reader who knows what is coming feels the weight of that.
passages.later:
The same care for the way to God's presence runs through the Old Testament. When the ark was later moved carelessly, a man died for touching it (2 Samuel 6:6-7).

The New Testament says that in Christ the distance has been closed: “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). The link is one of theme. This chapter is not a prediction, but it sets up the question the New Testament answers: how people may come near to a holy God and live.
passages.asks: The Levites stood guard so that God could live among his people without harm. Ask whether you treat God's nearness as a gift to be handled with care, or as something ordinary. And ask who has stood guard for you, by prayer or by teaching, so that you could come near.
